body:
Unpopular opinion:

The best career advice I ever got?

"Stop networking. Start helping."

Every meaningful connection I've made came from offering value first.

No expectations. No strings attached.

That's the secret nobody talks about.

3 years ago, I was mass-applying to 50+ jobs per week.

Zero responses.

Then I changed one thing:

I stopped being a resume.
I started being a story.

Instead of listing skills, I shared projects.
Instead of buzzwords, I showed results.
Instead of "experienced in X", I said "built Y that did Z".

Within 2 weeks, 5 interviews.

The job market isn't broken.
Your positioning might be.

I've reviewed 500+ LinkedIn profiles this year.

Here's what separates the top 1%:

1. They lead with outcomes, not responsibilities
2. Their headline is a value proposition, not a job title
3. They post consistently (even if it's just once a week)
4. They engage genuinely (not just "Great post!")
5. They tell stories that make you feel something

The algorithm doesn't favor luck.
It favors consistency and authenticity.

Which one are you working on?

I spent 6 months building something I'm really proud of.

A framework for writing LinkedIn posts that actually get seen.

Not engagement bait.
Not cringe humblebrags.

Just authentic content that resonates.

I've used it to grow from 500 to 15,000 followers.

And now I'm sharing it for free.

Drop a comment if you want the link.

Hot take:

Your resume doesn't get you the job.
Your story does.

Companies hire people, not paper.
